articles.title: DNI Warns Companies of Foreign AI Espionage - SuaraGarut.ID
articles.summary: DNI Warns Companies of Foreign AI Espionage  SuaraGarut.ID
articles.full_text:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned U.S. companies and the Trump administration Friday that foreign espionage targeting artificial intelligence is a real threat as the United States competes for leadership in the technology.
Clayton told CNBC that AI increases cybersecurity risks to interconnected U.S. digital infrastructure, including systems tied to public goods, national defense and global communications.
He said U.S. officials are focused on strengthening those systems and maintaining technological leadership against foreign actors.
"need to be wary" [sic] said Jay Clayton, Director of National Intelligence.
Clayton was responding to questions about the case involving Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, who was charged with allegedly installing a recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room.
Alfozan has not been charged with espionage. According to federal prosecutors, the former OpenAI employee had booked a one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member before his arrest.
"The short answer to your question is espionage, both commercial espionage, and I would say state-sponsored espionage, are realities," said Jay Clayton, Director of National Intelligence.
Clayton said the threat requires attention from both businesses and government because foreign efforts can target commercial and national interests.
"It's something that our private sector companies need to be wary of. We, as a government, need to be wary of," said Jay Clayton, Director of National Intelligence.
He said the OpenAI case illustrated the lengths foreign actors may pursue to challenge U.S. technological leadership.
"The OpenAI incident shows the lengths that people will go to try and supplant our leadership in this, or at least stay close to us in this emerging technology," said Jay Clayton, Director of National Intelligence.
An unnamed former CIA official told CNBC that the case may represent only part of a broader threat.
"probably the tip of the iceberg," said the former CIA official.
Clayton also described the first meeting of a White House AI task force, held Thursday, as a continuation of an accord signed by President Donald Trump and AI leaders at the White House the previous month.
"very good" said Jay Clayton, Director of National Intelligence.
Trump had described the agreement, which includes industry pledges to police AI risks itself, as "morally binding," according to CNBC.
The task force created three subcommittees covering reporting and response, critical infrastructure and private-sector coordination, and law enforcement and responsibility.
Clayton said the United States faces capable competitors across several countries as the AI race continues.
"We're not the only ones developing it. There are vectors in this technology that are coming from some of our known adversaries and competitors," said Jay Clayton, Director of National Intelligence.
He specifically cited China, Russia, Iran and North Korea as countries with significant technical capabilities.
"The Chinese, the Russians, the Iranians, the North Koreans all have significant technical capability. We need to stay ahead of them," said Jay Clayton, Director of National Intelligence.

articles.title: The Axis of Upheaval Goes to War
articles.summary: Andrea Kendall-Taylor and Richard Fontaine, former members of the National Security Council, argue that the members of what they call the “axis of upheaval”—Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea—are deepening their cooperation. Meanwhile, Washington is creating friction with many of its own partnerships. If these developments continue unabated, the United States will squander the strength of its network just as its adversaries learn to make the most of theirs.
articles.full_text:
On July 17, an Iranian missile struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, killing three American soldiers and wounding four others. The strike was unusually precise. In the weeks that followed, U.S. officials discovered that before the attack, Tehran had received high-resolution satellite images of the base that could aid its targeting. Afterward, Iran obtained more imagery, potentially helping it assess the damage and hone future attacks. The images came from Chinese entities.
China is not alone in assisting Iran. Russia, too, has helped Tehran find and hit American and allied targets. Two days before the March 27 attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia that wounded 12 American personnel, 14 Russian spy satellites passed overhead. U.S. officials later concluded that Moscow had fed Iran satellite intelligence that aided Iranian precision strikes. Moscow has also provided Iran with weapons and military expertise, including upgraded versions of Iranian drones refined on the battlefield in Ukraine, and Russian engineers are helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles that could evade U.S. and Israeli air defenses.
Neither Russia nor China has directly entered Iran’s war with the United States. They haven’t needed to. By providing intelligence on American targets, military technology and components, and economic and diplomatic support, they can give Iran what it needs without joining its war.
The United States entered the conflict with advantages its adversaries lacked: a vast network of formal allies, military bases, intelligence-sharing arrangements, defense partnerships, and interoperable forces spanning Europe, the Middle East, and Asia. Yet many of Washington’s traditional partners were reluctant to associate themselves with the campaign, and some denied the United States specific forms of military access, at least for a time. Others publicly resisted U.S. calls to help secure the Strait of Hormuz.
The contrast illustrates a striking shift since we first described Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea as an axis of upheaval in Foreign Affairs two years ago. The United States’ adversaries began this war with this weaker network, and Washington with the far stronger one. But after helping Russia fight its war in Ukraine over the past few years, members of the axis are now finding ways to make their network work in a new theater. They are fine-tuning their cooperation to make their partners more resilient—and more dangerous to the United States—while limiting costs and risks. Washington, for its part, is creating friction in many of its partnerships instead of deepening them, and risks squandering its network just as its adversaries are learning to make more of theirs.
SOURCES OF UPHEAVAL
Much has changed since 2024. Most obviously, the United States itself has become a source of upheaval in the international system. The Trump administration has challenged international institutions, strained traditional alliances, and adopted a more transactional approach to foreign policy. It has upended trade agreements, threatened the sovereignty of allies such as Canada and Denmark, and embraced unpredictability. It has also pursued improved relations with China, North Korea, and Russia while seeking to weaken Iran. None of this has loosened the ties among the United States’ adversaries.
Early in the Trump administration, U.S. officials expressed hope that normalizing relations with Moscow might peel Russia away from the group. Yet President Donald Trump’s oft-expressed bonhomie toward the Kremlin has opened no gaps with the other three. As seen from Moscow, the administration has been unable to deliver a deal on Ukraine, and any Trump-driven rapprochement with Washington is unlikely to endure: Congress continues to pressure Russia, and a future administration may well adopt a tougher approach.
More fundamentally, attempts to weaken the axis misunderstand what holds it together. Its members object to an international order that they see as enshrining Western dominance at their expense. But more pointedly, they oppose the United States’ extraordinary power to constrain, isolate, and punish them, and potentially to threaten their regimes. Recent U.S. actions have only rekindled those concerns. The United States’ capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and the killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei reinforce long-standing fears in Beijing, Moscow, Pyongyang, and Tehran about U.S. intervention and regime security.
The axis countries may moderate their anti-American rhetoric when doing so is tactically useful, but their motivation to reduce their vulnerability to American power remains. The Trump administration’s own skepticism about international order will not ease minds in axis capitals. On the contrary, Trump’s efforts to create a more transactional and coercive world may increase the value of their partnerships. As rules and institutions constrain less and brute power matters more, countries will seek partners to help them blunt sanctions, access critical technologies, compensate for military weaknesses, expand their room for maneuver, and resist isolation. Axis cooperation is evolving to meet the moment.
NEW REGIONS, NEW PROBLEMS
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, cooperation among the four countries was relatively easy to map. Iran provided Russia with drones, and North Korea sent ammunition, ballistic missiles, and later, troops. China became Moscow’s most critical lifeline, buying Russian oil and supplying the machine tools, microelectronics, and other components it needed first to sustain and then to expand its military production. Russia, in turn, transferred increasingly sophisticated military technology to its partners.
These exchanges were consequential, but they could still largely be understood as a series of bilateral transactions focused on Russia’s war. That is becoming less true. Cooperation is increasingly networked and geared toward solving new problems in new regions.
Russia’s drone program illustrates the change. Iran initially sold Russia its Shahed drones and then helped Moscow establish production at home. Russia did not simply replicate what it received; it incorporated Chinese components and continually modified the drones’ navigation, communications, payloads, propulsion, and tactics in response to Ukrainian defenses. New military units fed successful modifications back into production, generating an unusually rapid cycle of battlefield adaptation. Russia’s Unmanned Systems Forces, a drone-and-robotics branch of the Russian armed forces, was established last year to help institutionalize this cycle. The combination of domestic adaptation and axis partnership has proved effective. Russia’s latest jet-powered Geran drones, for instance, are faster, carry larger payloads, and are significantly harder for Ukrainian forces to intercept than earlier variants.
Russian improvements do not stay in Russia, either. They circulate through the axis network. For Iran, the technology that originally flowed to Russia is now returning, along with tactical advice drawn from Russia’s experience in Ukraine. If Russia’s jet-powered drones also show up in the Middle East, as they likely will, Iranian attacks on U.S. forces and regional energy infrastructure will become harder and costlier to defend against.
North Korea and China are also benefiting. According to Ukrainian reports, Russia struck a deal to help North Korea expand production of its Shahed-type drones. North Korean engineers have learned from time spent working in Russia’s massive Yelabuga drone factory, and North Korean forces fighting alongside Russia have gained firsthand experience in integrating drones into modern combat. Chinese military personnel have received training in drone warfare from Russian forces, and Chinese suppliers are gaining valuable information about how their technologies perform in combat. Beijing is thus seeing gains from the evolution of drone warfare that began with Iranian technology and has been refined in Russia’s war in Ukraine.
THE MODEL CAN TRAVEL
Two years ago, it was not clear whether partnerships among the four members of the axis could outlast the war that accelerated their formation. If the Ukraine war ended and Russia no longer needed Iranian drones, North Korean ammunition, or Chinese economic and technological support, the relationships might lose momentum.
Yet the war did not only create an immediate need for cooperation. It has also provided proof of concept for what these partnerships can accomplish, beyond what any country might attain on its own. Ukrainian defenses, Western sanctions, U.S. military supplies, and diplomatic isolation have all been less effective than would be the case if Russia were operating alone. By helping one another withstand pressure, the axis countries make it harder for the United States and its allies to compel them to change course.
Iran is now showing that the model can travel. Russia’s support for Tehran has been operationally meaningful but carefully bounded. Even as it fights its own war in Ukraine, Moscow has found ways to help Iran strike American targets and sustain the fight through diplomatic cover and material support while stopping short of actions that could draw Russia into direct conflict with the United States. China has been even more cautious, but its sharing of dual-use electronics and purchases of Iranian oil have similarly enhanced Iran’s ability to withstand U.S. pressure.
Such restraint is not evidence that the axis is weakening but rather a defining feature of how these partnerships work. With the striking exception of North Korean soldiers deployed on Russia’s behalf, the axis countries have generally avoided fighting one another’s wars. Instead, they provide political backing, economic support, intelligence, technology, and limited military assistance when doing so advances their own interests at manageable

articles.title: Russia's war reaches Bulgaria's shores, putting Radev's Moscow-friendly stance to the test - The Kyiv Independent
articles.summary: Russia's war reaches Bulgaria's shores, putting Radev's Moscow-friendly stance to the test  The Kyiv IndependentPutin brings war into Nato’s waters  The TelegraphDrone strikes in the Black Sea raise fears of Russian escalation to test NATO’s response  AP NewsBulgarian PM summons Russian ambassador after ship sinks in Black Sea drone attack  BBCBulgaria seeks NATO anti-drone systems, says defence minister  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev in Sofia, Bulgaria, on Oct. 6, 2026. (Nikolay Doychinov / AFP via Getty Images)
The balancing act of Bulgaria's Moscow-friendly leader stands on shaky ground.
Since taking office in May, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has taken a harsh line on Ukraine while adopting steps his critics say are accommodating to Moscow.
Radev's course has now come under scrutiny as Bulgaria, a southeastern NATO member state, feels first-hand the spillover of Russia's war against Ukraine.
Four merchant vessels were hit by drones near Bulgaria's Black Sea coast in October. Two of the vessels sank and several sailors are reported dead or missing.
Under fire from opposition, Radev, a former military officer and Bulgaria's ex-president, only cautiously hints at Moscow's complicity — stopping short of a direct accusation.
"Radev’s balancing act between the West and Moscow would eventually catch up with him."
With Russian drone incursions and Moscow-backed hybrid operations on NATO territory growing ever more brazen and frequent, Bulgaria has no guarantee that the strikes in its waters will come to an end.
Radev's room to maneuver between Bulgaria's NATO membership and a thaw in ties with Moscow is shrinking, observers say.
"I have argued for some time that Radev's balancing act between the West and Moscow would eventually catch up with him," Dimitar Keranov, an analyst at the German Marshall Fund's European Resilience program, told the Kyiv Independent.
"It now has."
Russia's war reaches Bulgarian waters
Two Turkish-managed ships were hit by naval and aerial drones about 70 nautical miles (130 kilometers) east of the Bulgarian town of Byala on Oct. 6, inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
The Alfa Watan, flying a Togo flag, sank, with 10 crew members — including nine Syrian nationals — presumed dead.
Two more vessels were hit by drones near the Bulgarian Black Sea coast on Oct. 13, including the Ukrainian-owned, Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, hit east of Byala. Its crew, including seven Ukrainians, was rescued.
The second ship, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity, was hit by drones east of the Bulgarian village of Krapets and sank, with 11 sailors reported missing.
The attacks came amid escalating hostilities in the Black Sea, with Moscow attempting to impose a blockade on Ukrainian trade by attacking ports and merchant ships.
Several commercial ships were also hit in and around Romanian waters over the past weeks.
While Ukraine has blamed Russia, Radev was initially hesitant to name the origin of the drones, saying only "they were clearly either Russian or Ukrainian."
Both Russian and Ukrainian drone incursions have been recorded along NATO's eastern flank over the past months, with the latter being a result of Russian jamming diverting Ukrainian unmanned vehicles.
But Radev's hesitation has provided an opening to the country's opposition.
On Oct. 6, lawmakers from the GERB–SDS, a center-right opposition coalition, blasted Radev for failing to properly identify the culprit.
The coalition's junior partner, the SDS (Union of Democratic Forces), even called the attack "an act of aggression by the Russian Federation in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone."
Finally, after the second attack, Radev acknowledged that Russia was the one to benefit from the attacks, and Sofia summoned the Russian envoy.
Nevertheless, Radev has not formally accused Moscow, citing a lack of decisive evidence.
Keranov summarizes this position as a "convenient deflection."
"Formal attribution takes time, but once a government concludes that the logic points to Moscow, it does not need a final forensic report to act on that assessment."
But Ruslan Stefanov, a program director and chief economist at the Center for the Study of Democracy, a Sofia-based European public policy institute, says waiting for proof is reasonable.
On the other hand, "continued failure to identify Russia as the main driver of instability and unsafe navigation in the Black Sea does not reflect operational reality and is widely seen as part of a broader pattern of unnecessary and harmful caution toward Moscow," he said.
"Moscow is testing Bulgaria because it sees it as the weak link on NATO’s southern flank."
The maritime attacks are not the only security-related incidents hitting Bulgaria in recent weeks and months.
Earlier in October, two masked men were said to have set fire to 11 out of 17 Starlink antennas at a facility near Sofia.
Ivaylo Mirchev, one of the leaders of the opposition Democratic Bulgaria (DB), hinted at connections to "Russian-style sabotage."
Yet Radev has remained tight-lipped about who was behind the arson, even though Poland blamed Moscow for a similar attack against a Starlink station on Polish territory in September.
Ukraine widely uses Starlink network services, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, for both civilian purposes and to support military operations.
And in August and September, explosions hit two arms facilities of the EMCO company, which supplies weapons to Ukraine.
The company called the September incident sabotage, while the Bulgarian Interior Ministry did not rule out either foreign interference or company neglect.
NATO's 'weak link'
As Bulgaria's president, Radev was ranked among the most Ukraine-skeptical voices in the EU — often compared to former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Since assuming the premier office, he has pulled Bulgaria out of the U.K.- and French-led Coalition of the Willing and halted arms supplies to Ukraine from Bulgarian army stocks.
He has also lambasted Western military aid for Kyiv, claiming it prolongs the war, and instead urged a diplomatic resolution.
At the EU level, Radev's government has blocked the inclusion of Moscow Patriarch Kirill in the 21st sanctions package and pushed to water down the EU's language on Ukraine's accession.
In light of these steps, drone strikes off the Bulgarian coast put Radev in an "uncomfortable position," Stefanov said.
"He built his campaign on the claim that there can be no military victory over Russia and that Bulgaria's interest lies in de-escalation," the expert noted.
"Those choices now raise the obvious question of why Bulgaria has not been spared."
Keranov believes that "Moscow is testing Bulgaria because it sees it as the weak link on NATO's southern flank."
Most NATO members along the alliance's frontier — from Romania to the Baltics — have already toughened their response to Russian provocations, with allied jets repeatedly downing invading drones.
Their leadership is also less reluctant to openly blame Moscow for the incursions.
While Radev's hesitation has provided ammunition to his domestic opponents, the prime minister's political position remains strong, Keranov said, adding that his popularity at home is not the real question.
"It is whether Bulgaria acts like a strong NATO member or keeps signaling indecision."

articles.summary: Grynspan leads after sixth UN Security Council vote — The National  UA.NEWS
articles.full_text:
In New York, United States, the UN Security Council held its sixth vote to select the organization’s next secretary-general. Costa Rican candidate Rebeca Grynspan retained a narrow lead, receiving nine favorable and five unfavorable votes, two of which came from permanent members of the Security Council.
As The National reports, Argentine Rafael Grossi and Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett each received eight favorable and six unfavorable votes. Each of them also received unfavorable votes from two permanent members of the Security Council.
Colored ballots
For the first time during the current selection process, Security Council members used colored ballots, which made it possible to separate the positions of the five permanent members — the United Kingdom, China, France, Russia, the aggressor state, and the United States — from the votes of the body’s ten elected members.
Before the vote, Panamanian President José Mulino said that his country would support Grossi. Panama is one of the non-permanent members of the Security Council. None of the seven candidates who took part in the October 16 vote withdrew their candidacy, and no new contenders emerged.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
US position and new candidates
Grynspan told Reuters that new names could enter the race after the vote and stressed that the process is not yet over. Minh-Thu Pham, co-founder of the Starling Institute and a former adviser to UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan, said that the gap between the three leaders had narrowed significantly and that there was no common position among the permanent members of the Security Council.
According to her, unfavorable votes are not equivalent to a veto, so the possibility remains for new candidates. At the same time, Pham warned that there is increasingly less time for new contenders to enter the race and win support in the Security Council.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said after the vote that Washington wants to see a strong and energetic leader at the head of the organization who will return the UN to its core mandate of maintaining international peace and security. He also said that the United States is primarily seeking the most qualified candidate rather than being guided by the principle of regional rotation or a candidate’s gender.

articles.summary: Pope urges humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky in call with Russian President  Vatican NewsPope Leo speaks with Putin from hospital, just days after lung cancer surgery  CNNPope calls Russian president Vladimir Putin urging Ukraine truce days after lung cancer surgery  Sky NewsPutin agrees to cooperate with Pope Leo's plea for aid for Ukrainian town  ReutersPope speaks to Putin from hospital, voices concern over Ukraine  The Washington Post
articles.full_text:
Vatican News
The Holy See Press Office released a statement on Friday afternoon, saying that Pope Leo XIV spoke by telephone with Vladimir Putin, President of the Russian Federation.
"During the conversation, the Holy Father expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and called for a ceasefire to allow the delivery of food and medical assistance, and the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population," said the statement.
"Finally, the Holy Father reaffirmed the Holy See’s commitment to promoting dialogue and peace," it concluded.
Pope Leo has been in Gemelli Hospital since Tuesday when he underwent an operation which removed the lower lobe of his right lung.
He previously spoke by phone with President Putin on June 4, 2025. The city of Oleshky lies along the frontline of the Russian-occupied Kherson region, on the banks of the Dnieper River.
Cardinal Parolin: Pope took initiative on behalf of besieged city
Afterwards, on the sidelines of a conference at the Catholic University of the Sacred Heart, Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin said, “It was the Holy Father who took the initiative to plead the case of this besieged city, where some 2,000 civilians need humanitarian routes through which they can leave.”
“The Pope called for a ceasefire to allow humanitarian aid, especially food, to reach the city and to enable those who wish to leave to be evacuated," he said.
“I hope that, in response to the Holy Father’s request, President Putin will agree to do what the Pope has asked,” Cardinal Parolin added. “The fact that he accepted the call and spoke with the Pope may, I hope, be a sign that the Pope’s request will indeed be carried out.”

articles.summary: Zelenskyy warns 20M Ukrainians could flee to Europe if Russia wins war  POLITICO.euZelensky praises ‘real leaders’ in Europe as his relationship with Trump deteriorates  CNNEU’s support to Ukraine matters more than ever, von der Leyen says, as US relationship sours – as it happened  The GuardianUkrainian President Zelenskyy speaks at EU summit amid spat with Donald Trump  DW.comEU rallies in support of Ukraine amid Trump standoff  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
BRUSSELS — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Friday that as many as 20 million Ukrainians could be forced to flee to Europe if his country falls to Russia.
“Russia is killing us,” Zelenskyy told reporters at a press conference on Friday during a summit of European Union leaders, adding Ukrainians were being “pushed” out of their country. “They [Russia] don’t want to stop.”
In the early days of Russia’s full-scale invasion, millions of Ukrainians fled their homes in Europe’s fastest and largest refugee crisis since World War II. Today, over 4 million Ukrainians live in EU countries under temporary protection status, with the largest populations in Germany, Poland and Czechia, according to Eurostat.
Zelenskyy’s stark warning comes as Ukraine heads into a brutal fifth wartime winter under Russian bombardment. Kyiv faces a budget shortfall of $30 to $35 million next year, according to projections from the International Monetary Fund — even accounting for a €90 billion loan Brussels agreed to provide last year.
The Ukrainian president traveled to Brussels to meet with European leaders and shore up financial support for his embattled country. While the EU is Ukraine’s staunchest backer, the bloc’s list of priorities is stacked with rising energy costs, looming elections, geopolitical crises and an impasse over its €2 trillion budget.

Iran’s apparent efforts to resume underground ballistic missile production and reports of Tehran mobilizing its regional terrorist proxies are putting Israel on high alert over the threat of a renewed multi-front confrontation in the Middle East.
New satellite imagery showing renewed tunneling and underground construction at three major Iranian sites — Parchin, Khojir, and Shahroud — has raised concerns about the Iranian regime’s efforts to rebuild its missile production capabilities despite Israeli and American strikes that severely damaged key facilities, according to a report released Wednesday by the Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI).
Experts note that the findings align with an earlier Wall Street Journal report indicating that Iran had resumed assembling ballistic missiles in underground facilities using components stockpiled before the war.
Even though all three sites remain heavily damaged, with rubble largely uncleared and restoration work limited, the report’s findings suggest Iran may be shifting some production and assembly operations underground to shield them from future attacks as tensions with Washington and Jerusalem remain high.
At Parchin, one of the three sites identified in the report and located southeast of Tehran, facilities used to produce solid rocket fuel remain damaged, with repairs underway following last year’s 12-day war.
Experts point out that restoring production will require clearing rubble, repairing damaged structures, and installing specialized equipment, suggesting that the facilities are still far from being fully operational.
However, the report identifies more substantial activity at the nearby Shahid Borujerdi tunnel complex, where satellite imagery shows the rapid restoration of a structure believed to provide electricity and other essential services to the underground facilities.
Experts also note tanks ranging from five to 13 meters long outside the tunnels, similar to those found at other Iranian missile production sites, suggesting the complex may be used to produce or assemble ballistic, cruise, or surface-to-air missiles, though this remains unconfirmed.
The second location, Hojir, a major defense complex southeast of Tehran, suffered extensive damage during the recent war, with both solid-fuel missile production sites still buried in rubble and facilities used to produce liquid-fueled missiles also heavily damaged.
FPRI’s findings challenge the Wall Street Journal‘s report that Iran has resumed underground missile assembly at Hojir, with researchers suggesting that if production has restarted, it may be taking place at a different, unidentified facility rather than the Shahid Muwahid complex.
The third location, Shahrud, a major solid-fuel missile production site in northeastern Iran, shows more progress in debris removal than Parchin and Khojir, with some damaged structures undergoing initial repairs, though extensive rebuilding and the installation of specialized equipment are still needed before production can resume.
Experts have also identified extensive excavation for a new tunnel complex in a mountain north of the production line, which they believe may be linked to Iran’s missile industry.
Even though the exact timeline remains uncertain, the report estimates that Iran could resume production within roughly a year if it concentrates restoration efforts at a single site and secures the necessary industrial equipment.
However, analysts warn that rebuilding the main factories may not be enough, as damage to other facilities that manufacture missile components could create bottlenecks and further delay the restoration of Iran’s missile production capabilities.
The reported findings cast partial doubt on earlier assessments that Tehran’s military infrastructure had been largely devastated during the war, suggesting that Iran’s defense industry was seriously damaged but not eliminated or unable to resume in some capacity.
According to another report published last week by the Institute for Science and International Security, satellite imagery has also revealed renewed activity at Minzadehei, a suspected nuclear weapons development site northeast of Tehran, with regular vehicle movements resuming after extensive cleanup efforts to clear debris and repair damage to the surrounding hillside.
Israeli officials have previously warned that Iran had restarted limited production of ballistic missiles, launch platforms, and anti-aircraft systems, relying on surviving components and production lines that escaped destruction or had already been restored.
Previous Israeli intelligence assessments also indicated that the regime had recovered missiles and launchers from underground tunnel systems damaged or rendered inaccessible during the conflict.
There is still no consensus on how long Iran’s reconstruction will take. Current estimates range from several months to several years, depending on the weapons system and the scale of foreign assistance Tehran is able to secure.
However, Israeli officials have warned that Iran’s reconstruction efforts are advancing faster than initial intelligence estimates had projected, as Tehran takes advantage of the ceasefire and ongoing diplomatic talks with the US to rebuild critical military capabilities.
These reconstruction efforts come as the threat of a broader regional confrontation looms, with Tehran reportedly instructing Lebanon-based Hezbollah, its chief terrorist proxy, to increase its military readiness for a conflict it considers “imminent,” raising fears of a wider escalation beyond Iran’s borders.
According to the Emirati news website Iram News, Iran is mobilizing its regional terrorist proxies and preparing them for a possible escalation of hostilities with Israel and the United States.
Unlike in the previous conflict, Hezbollah is reportedly preparing to adopt a decentralized combat system that would allow its forces on the ground to operate independently, even if Israeli strikes its senior leadership or cuts communication with central command.
Preparing for a possible escalation, the Iranian regime is not just funding its proxies and supplying weapons but also overseeing their military reconstruction and coordinating their readiness to ensure they can continue operating even if Iran’s senior leadership and military infrastructure come under attack, preventing a crippling blow to Tehran’s regional network.
Even with these efforts, experts note that Hezbollah has not necessarily regained its former military capabilities or its ability to shift the balance of power in the region. Rather, the move toward decentralized command is an attempt to address weaknesses exposed by Israeli operations.
In Israel, officials have warned of a “high probability” of attacks on civilians and renewed fighting, with security alerts expected to increase as election day approaches later this month for Israel (Oct. 27) and the US (Nov. 3) amid fears of escalation on multiple fronts.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz has requested an extension of the special state of emergency until Nov. 3, keeping emergency measures in place beyond election day amid ongoing security concerns.
On Wednesday, the Israeli defense chief issued a stark warning to Hezbollah, cautioning that any involvement in an Iranian attack on Israel would trigger a severe military response.
“If Hezbollah joins Iran in an attack on Israel, it will suffer a severe blow and lose more territory in southern Lebanon … which will become part of Israel’s permanent security zone. The Israel Defense Forces are prepared to carry out the maneuver,” he said.

articles.summary: Saudi Arabia says it thwarted a missile strike on Medina, and other Middle East developments  The Tribune-Democrat
articles.full_text:

Meanwhile, the Houthis claimed an attack in the Yemeni port city of Aden at a site used by the Saudi-backed and internationally recognized government, where officials said at least two people were killed. articles.title: Ukraine Is Hitting Putin Where His Data Lives - The Bulwark
articles.summary: Ukraine Is Hitting Putin Where His Data Lives  The BulwarkIs Zelensky right to say data centre strikes have taken down Russian bots?  BBCYandex outage: Data shows that instead of going dark, malicious bots went on the move  Cloudflare BlogData Centers Become Targets in Wars in Ukraine, Russia and the Middle East  The New York TimesUkraine Knocked Out Russian Data Centers. The Shutdown Revealed How Fragile Their Digital Infrastructure Is  Popular ...
articles.full_text:
DONALD TRUMP IS BACK to his favorite sport: throwing Ukraine under the bus. Last week, in his latest flareup of Putinophilia, he made an illegal deal to import Russian diesel fuel and unleashed his petulant rage at Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil facilities—which make Ukraine a convenient scapegoat for the spiking fuel prices caused by Trump’s bumbling war in Iran. Now, there are reported disruptions in Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the military-grade, Pentagon-controlled version of Elon Musk’s Starlink communications network. The United States may also have deliberately failed, on at least two occasions, to give Ukraine early warnings about incoming attacks. It’s difficult to avoid the conclusion that Ukraine is being stabbed in the back by its supposed ally. As the tart-tongued exiled Russian pundit Alexander Nevzorov put it on his YouTube channel, “Apparently, having figured out that he’s not strong enough to beat Iran, Trump decided to beat Ukraine.”
What makes this fiasco especially infuriating is that it takes place at a moment when the momentum tilts in favor of Ukraine, which has scored some impressive victories recently.
Most notably, while Ukraine may have suspended its strikes on Russian oil facilities to avoid angering Trump, its drones and missiles have been raining fury on a juicy new target: Russian data centers. The disruptions to every aspect of Russia’s digital infrastructure have been huge. And, while this infrastructure obviously supports Russia’s war effort in Ukraine, making it a legitimate target, the damage is inevitably causing a lot of pain to civilians, undermining the Russian war effort on the home front.
So far, Ukraine has struck three major data centers belonging to Yandex, a company sometimes described as “Russia’s Google” but in reality something closer to Google plus Amazon, Uber, PayPal, and iCloud rolled into one.1 All three facilities—including the two that house Yandex’s three “supercomputers”—were severely damaged; two came to a complete halt, wreaking havoc on servers.
Videos show Russians complaining about being unable to book a cab ride (many were reduced to trying to hail Yandex cabs in the streets), order a meal at a fast-food chain with a Yandex-powered register, make a medical appointment, or use the Yandex Pay service where all their money is stored. In one clip, a Russian woman who runs an online legal services firm says that not long ago, when Ukrainian strikes were taking out warehouses operated by Russian online retailers, she felt safe because her company had no physical products to warehouse. “Now it’s Yandex’s turn, and I see how wrong I was,” she says with wry resignation. Her company relies on Yandex Disk, Russia’s answer to Google Drive.
(In an interesting subplot to this story, there have been many reports that the disabling of Yandex data centers has resulted in a dramatic dropoff of pro-Russian and far-right propaganda, hate, and bot activity on social media. It would have been a great bonus. But alas, these claims—echoed even by Zelensky—seem too good to be true: investigations by the Guardian, France 24, and other media organizations show that they are based on unsourced or misinterpreted data.)
Yandex is working to restore access, using its still-functioning servers as well as those of other Russian corporations. But restoring the damaged facilities is likely to take months—especially since the company will be operating under sanctions that make it difficult to buy the necessary equipment abroad—and there is no guarantee that Ukraine won’t hit the centers again.
The delicious irony is that Russia’s digital infrastructure is especially vulnerable to attacks like this because of the Kremlin’s determination to control its subjects’ access to online information.
Russian data-localization laws require companies collecting Russian citizens’ personal data to use databases inside the country. Amendments passed last year tightened those requirements.
What’s more, the tendency of Russian business to “supersize it” means that, just as the country’s online retailers favor giant warehouses, its tech companies favor centralized, gigantic data centers. In the new drone-wars environment, these data centers are dinosaur-sized sitting ducks. And so far, they have remained largely unprotected—even after the warehouse strikes made it clear that the Ukrainians have no compunction about targeting facilities that operate primarily in the civilian economy.
Given such vulnerabilities, one would have thought the Russians would have been careful not to take the war to data centers. But they did—and bragged about it. In late September, Russia carried out a series of drone attacks on Ukrainian data centers and mobile phone networks in and near Kyiv, justifying these strikes on the grounds that the targets “process and transmit intelligence data for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.” The Russian Ministry of Defense then posted a snarky meme crowing about a “digital detox”—“on a mandatory basis.” But the “detox” was limited to temporary service disruptions for about 100,000 people. Even if Russia continues to target such facilities, Ukraine’s digital services are far more resilient than Russia’s because of Ukraine’s extensive use of hosts outside the country.
In a classic locking-the-barn-after-the-horse-has-bolted move, the Russian Duma is scrambling to save the data centers. Proposals include secret underground facilities—which, while theoretically feasible, would be tremendously costly and difficult. There’s also talk of changing the law to allow Russian internet traffic to be hosted in “friendly” countries like Belarus and Kazakhstan. However, it’s unclear whether the bandwidth capacity would be sufficient; to date, both countries have actually relied heavily on Russian servers for their own traffic.
Meanwhile, in the early hours of October 14, Ukrainian drones struck a “mega data center” operated by Sberbank, Russia’s de facto national bank with majority state ownership. While the data center was still under construction and not fully operational, users nevertheless reported encountering service outages for the banking giant.
What’s next? Expatriate Russian journalist-turned-YouTuber Dmitry Kolezev, who predicted attacks on Sberbank’s data centers less than twenty-four hours before the first such strike took place, says that Ukraine may further cripple Yandex by taking out its remaining large data center. (Unlike the other three centers, located in or near provincial cities 125 to 220 miles from the Russian capital, the still-intact data center is in Mytishchi, an industrial and residential city in the Moscow suburbs. Previous experience shows that Ukraine has had no trouble striking oil facilities on the outskirts of the capital.)
Kolezev also says that strikes on Sberbank data centers have the potential to bring the Russian economy to its knees—and, while Russia will try to boost air defenses for data centers, enough drones and missiles may get through to ensure that millions of Russians, and a lot of Russian businesses, will get their own long “digital detox.”
THE DATA CENTER HITS are not the only recent cause for Ukrainian celebration. The Ukrainian Armed Forces continue to push forward in the Donbas region while halting Russian advances; since May, Ukrainians have practically erased eighteen months of Russian gains near Lyman. According to veteran war correspondent David Axe, Ukrainian troops are now approaching the Zherebets River, a key strategic goal that would bolster Ukrainian positions near Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
What’s more, Ukrainian forces are inflicting far greater losses than they sustain. In September, according to a senior NATO official quoted by Bloomberg, Russian casualties exceeded 50,000, with some 28,000 dead—while Ukrainian losses totaled about 5,000. The approximately 10:1 ratio is especially remarkable given that Ukrainian troops are on the offensive on parts of the frontline. Recent Russian losses have also affected military elites: It is now confirmed that twenty officers, including seven colonels, were killed in one strike in Donetsk on August 26.
None of this means an easy road ahead. Almost every day, Ukrainian civilians have been killed by Russian strikes while Western help with air defenses has remained frustratingly inadequate—though Ukraine is having some success in building its patchwork defenses from a mix of homemade and imported technologies.
With no “energy ceasefire” in sight, Ukrainian cities brace for another winter of terror by cold. While some of the shortfalls in aid are caused by lack of hardware—producing enough armaments to meet Ukraine’s needs in a war that took Europe and the United States by surprise has been a logistical challenge, and Ukraine’s partners have their own defense requirements—there is also the question of political will.
But the new developments in U.S. behavior toward Ukraine on October 14 portend a new and very dark shift. Without warning, Starshield throttled its signal to moving units once their speed passed about 100 miles per hour, a limit typically exceeded by aerial drones. (There have been some reports of an even lower speed limit of about 40 miles per hour.) While Starshield connectivity reportedly does not disappear completely from the fast-flying drones, Ukrainian forces suggest it becomes unreliable enough to disrupt operations. As a result, Ukraine has said, several missions failed or had to be aborted. The extent to which this move was instantly unpopular across the board can be gleaned from the fact that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and the White House have been playing “it wasn’t me.”
This alarming news of alleged data throttling was exacerbated by the apparent withholding by U.S. intelligence of alerts about incoming Russian missiles. Zelensky, who has been extremely careful not to alienate Trump, has begun openly saying that Ukraine is “losing” America as a partner.

articles.title: French police accused over war-like injuries to teenagers in school protests | France - The Guardian
articles.summary: French police accused over war-like injuries to teenagers in school protests | France  The GuardianAre student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?  BBCFrance’s student uprising and young people’s mental health – what are the common causes?  The ConversationYellow Vests and high school students rally online ahead of October 17 protest  Le Monde.frFrance to witness a 'crossroads of anger' as mass protests expected on Saturday ...
articles.full_text:
French lawyers and rights groups have said that several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons used during school protests, and an unprecedented number of children have been held in police custody, some of whom reported being hit or racially insulted.
France is in the fourth week of its biggest youth protest movement in decades, during which hundreds of high schools across the country have been blockaded as students demand the replacement of absent teachers and repairs to decrepit buildings.
Police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of officer violence against demonstrators, including four children allegedly being “mutilated” by explosive weapons, and six sustaining “significant injuries”, as well as other complaints over physical blows, insults or alleged sexual assault, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, told the senate.
Evan, a 15-year-old studying carpentry at a vocational high school, had a hand blown off in the explosion of a police stun grenade outside a school protest in Lens, northern France, on 5 October. His lawyer, Bertrand Wattez, said: “His injuries resemble war injuries.”
Wattez said Evan had gone to school to attend class and discovered a protest under way. He said Evan had not taken part in violence and denied the Béthune state prosecutor’s assertion that the grenade had been picked up from the ground. When the grenade exploded, Evan lost his left hand, several fingers from his right hand and suffered injuries to other parts of his body. He remained in hospital “in a very difficult condition” and his family had filed a criminal complaint, Wattez said.
Another boy, Eden, 14 – who had been near a school protest in Saint-Ouen-l’Aumône, north-west of Paris – suffered extensive facial injuries, including two fractures to his jaw, the loss of his bottom teeth and all his top teeth broken after he was allegedly hit by a shot from a grenade launcher.
His lawyer, Elsa Marcel, said the shot from a grenade launcher was fired at close range, from a distance of 1.5 metres. “This is the equivalent of war weaponry,” she said. The family has filed a legal complaint for attempted murder.
Eden’s parents said he had gone to school but found it blockaded and had wanted to go home. Video footage appeared to show him facing three riot police officers. One officer hit out in his direction with a truncheon and Eden kicked in the direction of the police before a grenade shot was fired. An officer has been suspended and placed under official investigation.
This week, a police officer in the western city of Tours was charged with aggravated battery after Maël, a 16-year-old at a vocational high school, lost the use of his eye allegedly after a shot from a form of rubber-bullet launcher. The officer denies the charges. The family’s lawyer said Maël had not been involved in any violent confrontation with police but had simply been present at a school protest, and that the family felt a sense of “injustice”.
For several years, France has faced scrutiny over police use of explosive weapons, particularly after serious injuries were reported during the 2018-2019 gilets jaunes (yellow vests) street demonstrations, including allegations that people had lost eyes and had their hands and feet mutilated.
The current wave of protests has also led to lawyers raising concerns that an unprecedented number of children have been arrested and placed in police custody, with some lawyers reporting that teenagers said they were hit, humiliated or verbally abused during arrests.
Since the school protests began in mid-September, a total of 6,773 under-18s have been taken into police custody after they were arrested, the justice ministry said. For more than 1,000 of those children, no charges were brought; 2,190 are facing legal action and almost 2,000 were handed an alternative to further legal action, such as a citizenship course, without their case being heard at trial and without a conviction.
Lawyers said accusations against children included gathering with violent intent, violence against police and damage to property.
Nathalie Tehio, a lawyer and the president of the French Human Rights League, said the fact that only a minority of children’s cases would end up before a judge raised concerns that arrests could be unfounded. She said: “There are a record number of arrests … Often, the legal dossiers are empty. In reality, this is more about stopping people from demonstrating. I think there is a sense of hitting hard to try to dissuade people and scare them.”
Tehio said: “We have received accounts of racist comments made. Lawyers have told us that their clients say they have been humiliated or treated violently or pushed.”
Romain Boulet, a co-president of France’s Association of Criminal Lawyers, said: “Criminal lawyers are worried and raising concerns about the potential misuse of police powers to dissuade citizens aged under 18 from demonstrating.”
Mohamed Jaite, the president of the Paris branch of the leftwing union Syndicat des Avocats de France, has represented several teenagers stopped in Paris and its suburbs. “I have seen one youth limping in a police station,” he said. “Some have reported being humiliated or receiving racist and sexist insults.”
Prisca Ancion, a lawyer from the leftwing lawyers’ group Collectif d’Action Judiciaire, which demonstrated this week in front of a high school in Saint-Denis, in the northern suburbs of Paris, said: “There have been racist insults during arrests, as well as homophobic, sexist comments or sexual touching. We encourage families to file complaints.”
Another lawyer from the collective, Romane Bartoli, who assisted several teenagers after their arrest, said: “Youngsters told us they were slapped, kicked or punched.”
One 16-year-old from a high school in a suburb north of Paris described being arrested 100 metres from his school on the day of a blockade in late September. He plans to study medicine at university and said he had intended to go to class before he saw there was a protest.
Answering questions from the Guardian with his lawyer, he said he had been held in police custody for more than 12 hours, mostly with two others in a police cell with two mattresses.
“It was hard psychologically because I felt I hadn’t done anything wrong,” he said. “I was hit with a truncheon and punched.”
He said a police officer told him to “shut his mouth” and said: “It’s always you lot,” which he understood to be a racist insult. He was released after a state prosecutor instructed him to carry out a citizenship course as an alternative to facing legal action.
The justice ministry and the interior ministry, which oversees policing, did not comment on allegations of insults or violence in police custody.
In parliament, Nuñez denied any form of excessive policing or police repression. He suspended the use of stun grenades at school demonstrations.
Audrey Bailleul, a magistrate and national representative of the Union Syndicale des Magistrats, said it was hard to have a clear view of events at this stage. She said: “There is nothing to show that there has voluntarily been a massive intention to not respect [legal] procedure.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Lebanon's president on Thursday not to return several hundred kilograms of explosives which Lebanese authorities seized last week from the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah, a State Department official told CBS News.
In a call, Rubio asked Lebanese President Joseph Aoun "to hold accountable all those who ordered, financed, and directed the shipment, and underscored that returning explosives to Hezbollah should be out of the question," the official said.
The explosives had been seized on a road linking eastern Lebanon to Beirut, a Hezbollah lawmaker acknowledged earlier Thursday.

Rubio told Aoun the law is "routinely used for politicized prosecutions that deter steps towards peace," the official said. Mr. Trump set a precedent for using the MOAB, also known as the "mother of all bombs," when it was used in 2017 to attack an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds at a cost of $170,000 per unit.

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis are at War with Saudis for own Reasons, not as Iran Proxy - Informed Comment
articles.summary: Yemen’s Houthis are at War with Saudis for own Reasons, not as Iran Proxy  Informed Comment
articles.full_text:
By Laurent Bonnefoy, Sciences Po
(The Conversation) – A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s international airport has highlighted how the Yemeni group is reframing its perceived “Iran proxy” role and shifting its regional focus to its ongoing battle against Saudi Arabia. The Oct. 10 strike, in which 13 people were killed and hundreds injured, was the most violent episode on Saudi Arabian soil since the beginning of the war in Iran in February.
It was followed by further – albeit less deadly – missile barrages in the days since. The violence, moreover, comes just as the kingdom is hosting a major conference for oil producers.
As a longtime analyst of Yemeni politics, I see the latest attacks as another illustration of both the expanding regional stalemate across the Middle East and the need to understand how Yemen’s decade-long war is having effects far beyond its territory.
Houthi narratives
The Houthi movement first emerged as a militarized political actor in Yemen in 2004 and has been locked in a multiyear civil war against the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed central government. Currently, the Houthis control about a third of the territory and two-thirds of the population. They are undoubtedly Yemen’s most powerful armed force, despite lacking access to warplanes, and have developed an arsenal of long-range missiles and drones.
All along, the Houthis have frequently been portrayed by their adversaries and many external observers as a proxy for Iran, the chief regional rival to Saudi Arabia.
It’s true that the movement has long been broadly aligned with Tehran and frequently shared regional objections, even if the relationship is complex and varied. At the same time, the evolution of the Houthi movement remains intimately connected to Yemen’s domestic political context and to a historical feud specific to the country – something I and many other scholars have researched.
What is particularly significant in the current context of an escalating fight with Saudi Arabia, however, is the way in which the Houthi leadership has sought to reframe its military engagement over the course of 2026 so that it does not appear to be directed by Iran.
This shift is analytically important because it reveals how Houthi leaders understand the political effectiveness of particular narratives and how they seek to legitimize their actions.
A belated return to war
When the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran on Feb. 28, many observers expected the Houthis to enter the conflict swiftly. Their previous intervention in the Red Sea – between November 2023 and May 2025 – in support of Palestinians after Israel’s war in Gaza had, to some extent, provided a blueprint for disrupting maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The symbolic returns of their earlier campaign had been considerable. On the one hand, it demonstrated the Houthis’ willingness to act in support of Gaza at a time when many Arab governments were widely perceived as turning their backs on the plight of Palestinians. It also revealed the movement’s capacity to disrupt global supply chains and affect international trade far beyond Yemen.
But the Houthis remained on the sidelines for several months after the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Their leaders appeared to disregard reports that Iranian decision-makers had called on them, in July 2026, to close the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb to maritime traffic.
Assuming that the Houthis would automatically act at Tehran’s command reflected a misreading of Yemeni history and of the identity markers that shape the movement’s political legitimacy. Acting in support of Palestinians could be framed for a domestic and regional audience as an expression of Arab solidarity. But acting on behalf of Iran, a non-Arab Persian country composed almost entirely of Twelver Shia Muslims, was considerably more difficult to rationalize in Arab Yemen where Twelver Shia Muslims are absent and Sunnis are the majority.
The Houthis’ reentry into the regional conflict in August took place alongside a shift in their political narrative, which increasingly centered on their long-standing adversary, Saudi Arabia.
Although the strategic consequences of their actions may ultimately benefit Iran in its own regional and international conflicts, the Houthis see their military campaign against Saudi Arabia chiefly as an act of national defense.
An earlier airport bombing
During the summer of 2026, an important episode went largely unnoticed in the Western media: the Houthis’ attempt to establish the reopening of Sanaa International Airport through the surprise departure of a Tehran-bound flight and its subsequent return.
The airport, located in the Houthi-controlled capital, had been closed since late 2024 following Israeli strikes. Its continued closure meant that access to and exit from Houthi-controlled territory remained subject to restrictions imposed by the movement’s adversaries. These included the authorities controlling Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognized government.
From the Houthis’ perspective, their sovereignty consequently remained incomplete. The airport’s closure not only restricted civilian movement but also limited their ability to send supporters abroad for training and potentially to receive military equipment. On July 13, the Saudi military’s subsequent bombing of the Sanaa runway, as the incoming aircraft from Tehran approached, provided the movement an opportunity to reignite its confrontation with Riyadh.
After more than three years of a de facto ceasefire and difficult negotiations, Riyadh appeared, as in its dealings with Iran, increasingly eager to extricate itself from the region’s protracted conflicts. Sensing an opening, the Houthi leadership responded by invoking a logic of tit-for-tat retaliation.
The Houthis’ tactics today are a kind of mirror to the 2015 launch of a Saudi-led bombing campaign and blockade of the Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen that has led to years of protracted civil war. The Houthis now claim the right to impose reciprocal restrictions on Saudi Arabia, particularly by targeting its ports and oil-exporting infrastructure.
Saudi’s Houthi blowback
The Houthis’ new tactic serves two purposes. First, it allows the Houthis to redirect responsibility for the economic and humanitarian crisis in and around Sanaa toward the Saudi-enforced blockade rather than their own governance failures, mismanagement and corruption. Second, it provides a rationale for escalating the conflict across the region.
Previously, the Houthi military leadership had halted attacks on Israeli-linked shipping in the Red Sea following the formal Gaza ceasefire of October 2025, despite having repeatedly come under bombardment. It had likewise suspended attacks on American vessels following an agreement with the Trump administration in May 2025.
These decisions demonstrated a degree of pragmatism beneath the movement’s inflammatory rhetoric. That pragmatism appeared to persist even as the Houthis resumed their regional military engagement, with American diplomats reportedly meeting Houthi representatives in Oman in September 2026.
With Saudi Arabia, however, the Houthis felt less compunction. Riyadh was already facing repeated barrages of Iran missiles as a consequences of its alliance with the U.S. and facing an energy export squeeze. So with the Saudi airport incident, the Houthi leadership feels it has trapped Saudi Arabia, with consequences extending to the global economy.
This retaliatory strategy was bolstered by successful Houthi moves in early September to establish a degree of control over the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important maritime choke points. That gave the Houthis leverage over shipping crucial for Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea.
Drones and ballistic missiles, as the attacks on the Riyadh airport illustrate, also give the movement the capacity to strike targets across much of Saudi Arabia.
Photo by Mauro Lima on Unsplash 
The targeting of civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, particularly airports, illustrates the retaliatory logic the Houthis have invoked to justify their actions.
It’s far from clear what the consequences of this increasingly aggressive Houthi campaign will be. The region seems poised for ongoing strife, and it’s an open question whether it will draw back in the likes of the U.S., which has been reluctant to return to full-scale regional conflict.
Yet none of that should obscure the plight of civilians in Yemen. Rather, it should serve as a reminder of the suffering of a population exhausted by a war that has lasted for more than a decade and has devastated the already meager infrastructure of what was the poorest country in the Middle East even before the conflict started.

articles.title: The Nuclear Deal That Could Save NATO
articles.summary: Former U.S. NATO ambassador Ivo Daalder argues that the scramble to shore up Europe's conventional defense risks overlooking the continent's greatest security weakness: nuclear deterrence. Europe knows it can't fully trust Washington's guarantee anymore. But he lays out a middle path between dependence and nuclearization that would extend France's and the United Kingdom's nuclear umbrella—a course, he argues, that could even repair the transatlantic alliance.
articles.full_text:
At a meeting earlier this year, top foreign ministry officials from several European countries were asked who among them still believed that the United States would come to their defense if they were attacked. Not a single hand went up. It was a stark indication of the extent to which European governments have concluded that the United States—for so long the backbone of European and NATO security—is no longer a reliable ally. Over the past 18 months, conversations in Brussels and in other NATO capitals have revolved around how to boost the continent’s conventional defense to make up for Washington’s retrenchment. But a quieter and more urgent discussion is also taking place, focused on the status of the ultimate deterrent: the U.S. nuclear guarantee.
More than half a century ago, the Great Debate, as the French strategist Raymond Aron termed it, broke out between European countries and the United States over how to preserve European nuclear deterrence in the face of the Soviet Union’s expanding nuclear capabilities. Then, European leaders feared that Washington’s growing emphasis on the conventional defense of the continent reflected an increasing reluctance to protect Europe with nuclear weapons—especially as Moscow developed missiles that could reach the U.S. homeland. Would the United States be willing to risk Boston to defend Berlin? That debate was ultimately resolved through a new grand bargain: in return for a commitment from European countries to forgo developing nuclear weapons, the United States would invite more European participation in nuclear decision-making. That essential bargain stuck for 60 years, helping secure both the United States and Europe and preventing nuclear proliferation.
Now, however, that bargain has come undone. Washington says that it wants a new division of labor: the Europeans need to take on primary responsibility for their conventional defense while the United States continues to ensure their nuclear defense. But that hardly addresses the problem. “If you don’t believe in the United States’ Article 5 commitment,” one of the officials attending the meeting told me, “then extended deterrence is effectively dead.” Already, alternative options are being considered. In some European capitals, officials are quietly raising the possibility of acquiring their own nuclear weapons. France, meanwhile, has offered to adapt its nuclear policy to help defend its European allies.
Each of these options has real logic. But none of them adequately addresses the problem of ensuring European security without risking further proliferation. A better approach would be a fourth alternative: a renewed U.S.-European nuclear bargain, this time with a real European core. Led by France and the United Kingdom, NATO’s European members need to take on a larger role in their nuclear deterrence while working to restore the transatlantic defense link that has been the foundation of U.S. and European security for so many decades.
FOUNDATION OF PEACE
The Soviet Union’s 1957 launch of the Sputnik satellite posed a profound dilemma for NATO. Until then, the alliance had counted on U.S. nuclear weapons deployed in Europe to deter an attack by a much larger Soviet conventional force. But once Moscow demonstrated its ability to launch intercontinental rockets, Europeans feared that the United States would no longer be willing to use nuclear weapons to prevent a Soviet invasion of Europe.
These concerns prompted a fierce debate within NATO about how the continent could ensure its nuclear defense. Some, led by France, were convinced that European countries needed their own nuclear weapons. Others sought less costly ways to restore some control over nuclear deterrence. One American idea that gained substantial traction was to create a so-called multilateral force—a fleet of vessels carrying some 200 missiles. Such a multilaterally operated and funded force could give Europeans a sense of ownership and control over the use of nuclear weapons, the thinking went, while preserving the U.S. president’s final authority over their launch.
The debate exposed a fundamental problem with extending U.S. nuclear deterrence to allies, especially if an ocean separates those allies from Washington. An adversary might be deterred from attacking an American ally by even the small possibility of a U.S. nuclear retaliation; the consequences of a miscalculation would be catastrophic. But that same small possibility would offer little comfort to the ally, who needs to believe that Washington would actually risk nuclear devastation on its behalf. Denis Healey, the United Kingdom’s defense secretary throughout much of the 1960s, postulated what became known as the Healey theorem: “It takes only a five percent credibility of American retaliation to deter an attack, but it takes a 95 percent credibility to reassure the allies.”
 The Sputnik launch posed a profound dilemma for NATO.
The debate was ultimately resolved through a bargain. Washington’s European allies agreed to forgo their right to acquire nuclear weapons in return for a greater say in U.S. nuclear weapons policy and strategy. Although the idea of a costly multilateral force was abandoned, the creation of the NATO Nuclear Planning Group (NPG) provided a vehicle for Europeans to give input into U.S. nuclear planning and for Washington to demonstrate that European security interests were integral to its nuclear strategy and force posture. Reassured, European countries (aside from France and the United Kingdom) agreed to codify their nonnuclear status in the 1968 Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty.
Many European countries retained ground- and air-based systems that could deliver U.S. nuclear weapons deployed on their territory. Today, about half a dozen European countries still deploy dual-capable aircraft that can carry U.S. B-61 nuclear bombs. These nuclear consulting and sharing arrangements proved far more crucial to reassuring allies than the hard-power measures (such as counterforce targeting, low-yield weapons, and greater precision) that U.S. strategists typically believe were essential. The latter measures focused on resolving the five-percent problem; the former addressed the 95-percent questions.
France was the only country to reject this nuclear bargain. (The United Kingdom had become a nuclear power in the 1950s, but it committed all its weapons to NATO and participated in the NPG and the dual-capable aircraft missions.) Under President Charles de Gaulle, France came to believe that it could not count on another country for its nuclear security. Paris embarked on its own nuclear program, refused to participate in the NPG or the dual-capable aircraft mission, and, in 1966, withdrew from NATO’s military command structure. The overall bargain, however, laid the foundation for what has become a highly successful deterrence, reassurance, and nonproliferation regime.
DEAL BREAKER
Unlike in the 1960s, today’s nuclear debate has not been prompted by a change in the global balance of power. It has been precipitated by a unilateral change in the United States’ attitude toward Europe. As I explained in Foreign Affairs last year, in Trump’s second term, the United States has rejected the two core principles of NATO’s collective defense commitments: that there is a shared understanding of the threat to NATO members and that members’ security is indivisible.
European members of NATO can no longer assume that the U.S. commitment to their security—derived from the fundamental idea, born of two devastating world wars, that American security is inextricably linked to the security of Europe—is ironclad. Instead, as the Pentagon’s policy chief, Elbridge Colby, has repeatedly noted, “under President Trump’s leadership, the simple fact is that countries can no longer take America for granted.” European countries have never taken America for granted. They have assumed that it shares their belief in the indivisibility of U.S. and European security—and they proved their own commitment to this belief when NATO invoked Article 5’s collective-defense obligation for the first and only time, in response to the September 11, 2001, attacks on the United States.
The American president and other senior officials have made it clear that the United States’ security commitment to Europe is based not on a shared understanding of the threat that both entities face but on secondary considerations, such as European countries’ level of defense spending and their support for U.S. foreign policy. In August, the Pentagon sent its 31 NATO allies a long questionnaire stressing the conditionality of Washington’s security commitment: it asked them to profess their loyalty to Trump’s foreign policy, commit to procuring defense equipment from U.S. firms, and prioritize funding the restoration of the U.S. industrial base by opposing any “buy European” initiatives.
Some European NATO leaders still refuse to admit in public that anything fundamental has changed. Privately, though, most have reached the same conclusion as senior European political officials: that the United States can no longer be counted on to come to Europe’s defense. And if that is true when it comes to conventional defense, it is even more true with respect to the nuclear guarantee. That leaves Europe facing questions it has never had to ask before. What if Russia attacked NATO territory and Washington told Europe it was on its own? How would nonnuclear allies stand up to a nuclear-armed Russia? What if Moscow used nuclear threats, implicit or explicit, to try to force Europe to end its support for Ukraine? None of these scenarios are far-fetched. Russia has issued veiled nuclear threats against Europe repeatedly since 2022, most recently in September, after NATO conducted air exercises above northeastern Poland, near Kaliningrad.
FOOL’S BARGAINS
