EU leaders stuck to their red lines on the next long-term budget at Thursday's summit, with several now rejecting the presumed December deadline. Council President António Costa is now expected to take over the negotiations, with a new compromise due in a few weeks.
EU leaders have refused to budge on the bloc’s next long-term budget and openly cast doubt on whether a deal can be sealed by the end of the year, a slippage that would mean significant delays and a collision with a string of national elections.
Until now, capitals were committed to reaching a final agreement by December 2026. But at Thursday’s summit in Brussels, where talks dragged longer than expected, a growing number of governments are asking whether that is really necessary.
"We are not reaching an agreement this month. Not next month. I don’t know even if it’s possible to reach an agreement before the end of the year," said caretaker Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. "I think we are not in a hurry."
For months, European Council President António Costa has repeated that leaders must unanimously agree the next seven-year budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), by December at the very latest.
If talks spill into 2027, he warns, there will not be enough time to complete the complex legislative work needed to get the budget up and running by 1 January 2028.
Following the inconclusive summit, where the Irish presidency’s compromise proposal to cut the overall volume by €141 billion was largely rejected, Costa will take over the negotiations, which was largely expected.
The European Council President is due to present a new negotiating proposal in a few weeks, which is bound to follow a completely different logic from the Irish one. EU leaders have been called in for a special summit on 26 November.
In particular, Costa's proposal is due to keep the national contributions low, a new package of EU-wide taxes to finance the budget, and maintain sufficient flexibility for unforeseen expenses, a budget line the Irish proposal significantly cut down.
Already before the summit, the draft joint conclusions were watered down concerning the deadline, softening language that explicitly set out “the aim of reaching a final agreement by the end of the year.”
By contrast, the final language says that "an agreement before the end of 2026 would allow for the adoption of legislative acts in 2027, which is necessary to ensure that EU funding reaches beneficiaries without interruption in January 2028."
Speaking before the summit, several leaders made clear that they do not feel bound by an end-of-year timeline, as it would be extremely difficult to explain to their domestic audiences that they accepted a bad deal because of an artificial deadline.
"The date cannot become more important than the content," Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told the Senate on Wednesday.
"We will not sign an agreement that is not advantageous to us just to meet a deadline. We will sign an agreement only when it is right for Italy."
There is, however, no consensus on what a “good deal” looks like. Every government wants to take as much as possible from the EU budget while paying in as little as possible.
The main battle line runs between two camps: the so-called “frugals,” a German-led coalition of six net contributors pushing for steep cuts to the overall volume, and the Friends of Cohesion, a 17-strong bloc of southern and eastern countries fighting to preserve traditional funding programmes for the poorest regions.
But the camps are not monolithic. Some Friends of Cohesion, like Spain and Italy, have a vested interest in agricultural funds. Others, like the Baltic states, want to boost defence spending due to their proximity to Russia.
Among the frugals, Germany and Sweden are seen as the most radical, while Finland is keen on farming subsidies. France, the bloc’s second-largest economy, has yet to pick a side, trapped between its European ambitions and a runaway budget deficit.
Belgium and Luxembourg are somewhere dithering between the factions.
"In the end, we need a good Multiannual Financial Framework. So, of course, everyone wants to make speed. But it’s more important to have a good deal than a bad deal," Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said.
In other words, the red lines are so entrenched, and the room for compromise so slim, that a landing zone currently looks like a mirage.
In Brussels circles, deals on sensitive topics are only struck under intense time pressure, because neither side feels compelled to make concessions until the last minute. Signalling that one does not feel bound by a timeline may therefore be a negotiating tactic to stand one’s ground.
For EU officials, even more worrying than the potential delay to funding programmes are the string of elections due in 2027 in France, Italy, Poland, Finland, Estonia, Slovakia and Greece. Some fear that if no deal is reached by the end of this year, it could slip to autumn 2027.
Paris is a particular concern. Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is currently the favourite to win the presidential race, and she has promised to cap France’s contribution at €5 billion a year, a sharp cut from the current level of around €8 billion.
Meanwhile, elections in Spain, where voters go to the polls on 29 November, and Sweden, which voted in September, "are likely to create some issues", said Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides.
Christodoulides reiterated the need to reach an agreement by the end of the year. He is one of the few EU leaders still saying so.

articles.title: Pope speaks with Putin, denouncing recent attacks as he shows recovery from lung surgery progressing - AP News
articles.summary: Pope speaks with Putin, denouncing recent attacks as he shows recovery from lung surgery progressing  AP NewsPope Leo speaks with Putin from hospital, just days after lung cancer surgery  CNNPutin agrees to cooperate with Pope Leo's plea for aid for Ukrainian town  ReutersPope urges humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky in call with Russian President  Vatican NewsPope speaks to Putin from hospital, voices concern over Ukraine  The Washington Post
articles.full_text:
ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV gave strong indications Friday that he was recovering well from lung cancer surgery and was very much in charge of running the Catholic Church, speaking on the phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, meeting with top aides and celebrating Mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.
The Vatican said that during the call with Putin, “the Holy Father expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and called for a ceasefire to allow the delivery of food and medical assistance, and the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population.”
The statement added that Leo “reaffirmed the Holy See’s commitment to promoting dialogue and peace.”
The statement was significant, showing Leo was well enough to conduct official diplomatic business from the Gemelli hospital, was keeping up with world events and was continuing to promote his message of peace as he recovers from surgery. The Kremlin readout of the call suggested progress had actually been made on the humanitarian front.
The Kremlin said Putin wished Leo good health and a quick recovery. In response to the pope’s concern about the plight of civilians in the frontline town of Oleshky, Putin gave a “detailed explanation regarding the Kyiv regime’s responsibility for the difficult humanitarian situation there,” the Kremlin said in a statement.
Putin voiced support for “the Vatican’s intention to help create conditions for ensuring the safety of the local population and facilitating the delivery of essential supplies,” and an agreement was reached to coordinate efforts in this regard, the statement said.
Mass and a homily thanking hospital staff
Also Friday, the Vatican released the first images of Leo since his lung cancer surgery Oct. 13, showing him standing up at the altar in green vestments, as doctors said that tests confirmed his “continued improvement.”
The 71-year-old Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
“His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own,” said a medical update signed by Leo’s personal physician Dr. Luigi Carbone and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
Leo presided alone over the liturgy, distributing Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present, Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said. He also delivered a homily in which he thanked the hospital staff “for the work they do every day taking care of the sick in their fragility, and in a particular way what they had done for him,” Bruni said.
Bruni confirmed Leo would deliver the traditional noontime Angelus prayer on Sunday, but it wasn’t clear whether he would do it from the hospital or back at the Vatican.
The Vatican had originally estimated a weeklong hospital stay, and had cancelled his audiences through Tuesday. Bruni said the pope’s doctors would decide if there were any changes expected to his discharge date.
But with Leo’s homily Friday thanking hospital personnel who had cared for him, there might be little reason for him to stay if he was medically ready for discharge.
A signal of all systems go for trip
Even as questions swirled about the future of Leo’s young pontificate, there were signs Friday that it was all systems go. The Vatican published the names of journalists accredited to fly on Leo’s plane with him during his Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
Leo’s ability to make the trip has been in question since his diagnosis, and the Vatican can change the plans at any time. But the posting of the media list signaled that at least on an organizational level, the trip was going ahead.
Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular and genetic makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary.
Secretary of state suggests ‘adjustments’
The Vatican secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, said Friday he understood Leo’s recovery was going well, “so we’re happy.”
Parolin was considered a leading contender in the conclave that elected Leo and was recently passed over as dean of the College of Cardinals. He surprised some by suggesting Thursday that Leo’s pontificate itself might need to be “adjusted” as a result of the cancer. It was a bold statement coming from Parolin, given the indications that Leo was recovering well.
On Friday, Parolin seemed to roll that back. Asked what he meant, Parolin said “adjust on the basis of his health conditions,” at least “with respect to this next trip.”
Parolin spoke to reporters outside a conference at the Sacred Heart University, of which the Gemelli hospital is part.
Though Parolin was nearby, there were no signs Parolin visited Leo as might be expected.
The Vatican said two other top cardinals did call on the pope instead Friday: Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the pope’s vicar for Rome, and Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, who was recently elected dean of the College of Cardinals, a position that many had thought would go to Parolin, 71. Leo confirmed Tagle in the job two days before announcing his surgery.

Abstract
Coral reefs are diverse marine ecosystems that provide ecological functions and economic and social benefits across over 100 tropical countries.
Warming driven by climate change is a primary threat to coral reefs and is increasing the frequency of global coral bleaching events.
Here we reassessed the IUCN Red List status of 892 reef-building coral species, first assessed in 2008 1.
Because species-level population trends are unavailable for most reef-building corals, population reductions were inferred using proxies based on global coral cover trends and projected annual severe bleaching under SSP2-4.
5, both over three decades, adjusted using trait-based estimates of species vulnerability.
Of the 774 species with sufficient data to be assessed, 340 (44%) were classified as threatened under IUCN Red List criteria.
Thirty-three species were assessed as Critically Endangered, 251 as Endangered, and 56 as Vulnerable, most due to risk of population reduction associated with projected thermal stress.
These findings predate the three hottest years on record and the fourth global coral bleaching event (2023-2025), and the first exceedance for an annual mean of the 1.
5oC global warming threshold.
The findings reinforce the importance of limiting further warming to maintain coral biodiversity and reef ecosystem function.
The Red List assesses the relative extinction risk of species, whereby species are placed in categories of increasing risk by comparing their population size, decline and geographic range against standardised thresholds.
The Red List does not predict whether or when a species may go extinct.
As the ranges of coral species remain under-surveyed, future assessments would be strengthened by species-level population data and thermal-stress and recovery metrics that better capture range-representative dynamics.

Ukraine is resuming strikes on Russian oil refineries, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced.
Zelensky said Ukraine had held off on striking Russian oil refineries for three days at the request of U.S. President Donald Trump.
Russia, meanwhile, had not honored the so-called energy ceasefire, Zelensky said, continuing to strike Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and killing about 100 civilians over the past week.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” the Ukrainian president said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday morning, October 15.
The first strike by Ukraine’s military after the pause appears to have hit the Ryazan oil refinery. The plant, owned by Rosneft, is one of the key fuel suppliers for Moscow and the Moscow region.
Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov announced the morning of October 15 that classes had been canceled in 14 schools and 25 kindergartens in Ryazan because of “a mass drone attack on the region.” The Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ published a photo early that morning showing a flare over the Ryazan oil refinery, suggesting it was linked to the drone attack.
Authorities in the Ryazan region confirmed the strikes, saying a fire had broken out at the refinery. Malkov also said that “a warehouse and vehicles on the grounds of another enterprise in Ryazan” had been damaged. He declined to give further details, adding that the damage was being assessed.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said Ukraine’s military attacked the Ryazan oil refinery with 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. The Russian military said it had shot down the drones and missiles, but added that “a fire broke out at the refinery as a result of falling drone debris.”
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Wednesday afternoon, October 14, that Ukrainian forces had struck two oil refineries, one in the Saratov region and one in the Ryazan region. “We see that the Ukrainian side is not showing any movement toward an energy ceasefire,” he said. At the time, authorities in the Ryazan region and eyewitnesses had not reported any strike on the refinery there, and Novak’s claim about a strike on an oil refinery in the Saratov region remains unconfirmed.
Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov, commenting on Zelensky’s remarks about resuming strikes, referred to Novak’s statement. According to Peskov, there had been no moratorium on Ukraine’s part, and strikes on Russian oil refineries and energy facilities had continued throughout this period. “There is nothing new here,” Peskov said, once again accusing Ukrainian authorities and Zelensky personally of “not wanting to make peace.”
War in photos. Aftermath of a Russian strike on Kyiv.
Russian forces struck Kyiv with drones and missiles overnight on October 14, killing three people and injuring about 20. A nine-story apartment building caught fire in the Desnianskyi District as a result of the strike.

articles.title: The Houthis are Europe’s problem - The Telegraph
articles.summary: The Houthis are Europe’s problem  The TelegraphWhat do the Houthis want?  Financial TimesHow the Houthis are helping Iran turn Saudi Arabia into a pressure point  ReutersIran cultivated Houthis for years before opening new war front, Yemeni insider says  Iran InternationalWhy not deal with the Houthis instead of fighting them?  アラブニュース
articles.full_text:
The level of sophistication demonstrated by the latest Houthi missile attacks against Saudi Arabia does not just signal a serious upgrade in the military capabilities of an organisation once regarded as a rag-tag terrorist group. It begs the question of why the West is not doing more to support its Saudi allies. The Houthi attacks threaten to cause even greater disruption to global energy supplies, with all the implications that could have for already hard-pressed Western economies – including the UK.
The latest Houthi attacks on the Saudis represent a major escalation in the threat they pose to regional stability. In the decade or so since the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels provoked Yemen’s disastrous civil war by attacking the country’s democratically elected government, the Houthis tended to rely more on basic weaponry, such as rocket-propelled grenades and the ubiquitous Soviet-era AK-47 assault rifles. That is now very much no longer the case.
Fourteen people have so far been killed in the Houthi missile strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, which succeeded despite the Saudis’ sophisticated anti-missile defences. The headquarters of the Saudi state oil giant Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran were also hit. Several further Houthi missile strikes were intercepted, the Saudis confirmed.
The Houthis claim they launched the attacks in retaliation for what they call “brutal Saudi aggression” in western Yemen, where the Kingdom’s forces are fighting to reclaim territory recently captured by the terrorists in their bid to seize control of the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which is the southern entrance to the Red Sea. But the Saudis, together with their Gulf allies, are under no illusions that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is behind the attacks as they seek to increase their stranglehold over global energy supplies.
Having succeeded in causing severe disruption to the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf, which in normal times carries around one fifth of the world’s energy needs, the IRGC believes it can increase the pressure on global economies if it can use its Houthi allies to simultaneously disrupt shipping heading for the Suez Canal.
There is no doubt that the IRGC is deeply involved in supporting the Houthi attacks. Missile fragments recovered by the Saudis from previous Houthi attacks have carried unmistakable Iranian markings. Yet, rather than scrambling to support their Saudi allies, Western leaders appear strangely reluctant to provide Riyadh with effective military backing, an oversight that seems all the more unfathomable given that the upsurge in Houthi attacks is ultimately as disruptive for the West as the Saudis.
Donald Trump’s preoccupation with next month’s midterm elections means that he is unlikely to approve any meaningful military response to the Houthis’ aggression, despite reprimanding the group for “behaving very badly”. Nor are there any indications that other Western leaders are willing to come to the Saudis’ aid.
Andy Burnham was happy to utter his predictable platitudes in the Commons earlier this week, declaring that “we will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis”. But that support amounts to little more than the temporary loan of a single air refuelling tanker, as well as some air defence assistance.
Other European countries are similarly proving reluctant to deploy military assets, with only the Netherlands and Belgium responding to appeals from Brussels to strengthen the EU’s Red Sea Naval mission. This force still does not have enough warships to fulfil its stated mission objective of safeguarding the Bab el-Mandeb.
The West’s underwhelming response bears little comparison to the robust action mounted in 2024, when the Houthis first attempted to disrupt merchant shipping in the Red Sea, claiming they were acting in support of Hamas terrorists in Gaza. While the US deployed a naval battlegroup, the UK dispatched a destroyer and launched air strikes against Houthi positions from the UK’s Akrotiri base in Cyprus.
The Israelis too, proved to be effective allies in that campaign, regularly launching airstrikes against Houthi positions. After Ed Miliband’s pointless diplomatic spat with the Israelis over imposing sanctions against Israeli settlements, any future UK cooperation with Israel on tackling the Houthis is out of the question.
The West’s reluctance to provide the Saudis with tangible support is short-sighted, especially for the European leaders who need to understand that the Houthis’ decision to escalate their attacks against the kingdom is as much a problem for Europe as it is the Saudis themselves.
With European countries – including the UK – already anticipating an energy crisis this winter, the prospect of rising bills and power shortages will become ever greater the longer the Houthis and their Iranian-backers are allowed to implement their plan to disrupt global shipping.
Burnham and his fellow European leaders need to understand that, by failing to confront foes who threaten their countries’ interests, they are demonstrating a level of weakness that their enemies will be only too eager to exploit.

articles.title: ‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentary - The Guardian
articles.summary: ‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentary  The GuardianA Gaza war documentary sparks outrage in Israel  NPRNAZA film review — Israeli accounts of assault on Gaza make brutally hard viewing  Financial TimesNetanyahu demands probe into sources for award-winning Gaza film NAZA  Al JazeeraI survived Gaza's horrors. I watched NAZA to learn how Israeli soldiers live with it  Middle East Eye
articles.full_text:
Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.
NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was released in UK cinemas this week and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.
The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise.
In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus”.
British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.
Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.”
The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”.
The Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an exposé” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”.
The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.”
The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”.
The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.
When the film opened in Italy last month, it topped the charts. The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”.
The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.
Various organisations, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize.

articles.summary: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role  BBCUkraine advances in occupied Donetsk as Trump hands Putin diesel deal  Al JazeeraOperation Vivaldi: success of Ukraine’s counteroffensive shows it has learned to manoeuvre on a drone-filled battlefield  The ConversationUkraine says it frees more territory in Donetsk region counteroffensive  ReutersUkraine reports more battlefield gains as Putin’s invasion loses momentum&n...
articles.full_text:
Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role
- Published
A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.
Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.
This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.
The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.
While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September – and suffered few casualties in return.
The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".
Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.
He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.
This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.
Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.
Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.
Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.
Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.
Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.
The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.
An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."
He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.
Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".
"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."
Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.
In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.
"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."
"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".
That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.
"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.
"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."
All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.
This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin.
Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.
But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.
The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.
I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."
Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko

articles.summary: '‘It’s easier dealing with Trump than Putin,’ Zelenskyy tells Euronews amid US tensions  EuronewsZelensky: My people are dying after Trump’s Starlink betrayal  The TimesThe new unequivocal Zelenskyy  Financial TimesZelensky’s despair as Trump turns towards Russia  The IndependentZelenskyy on Trump saying Putin is easier to negotiate with: I find him easier than Putin  Українська правда
articles.full_text:
After a week of tensions between Washington and Kyiv, Zelenskyy said Trump was still easier to deal with than Putin, despite the US president’s calls for new leadership in Ukraine and criticism of the Ukrainian leader.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected Donald Trump's claim that he is more difficult to deal with than Vladimir Putin, telling Euronews that negotiating with the US president is easier than dealing with the Russian leader.
Speaking to Euronews on Friday at an EU summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy was asked about Trump's criticism and whether European leaders supported Ukraine's continued strikes on Russian oil refineries despite pressure from Washington to halt them.
"Well, it's easier dealing with him than with Putin. I'm talking about Trump," Zelenskyy said.
"I've had several meetings with the President of the United States of America, and we always find topics for discussion and decision-making."
The remarks come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure and Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel. The US president has criticised the strikes, blaming them for contributing to rising global fuel prices.
Zelenskyy said his priority was to defend Ukraine's national interests, regardless of external pressure.
"I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively. We were attacked, occupied, and our people were killed. It is only logical that we have the right to defend ourselves," he said.
"This is entirely lawful, and so we will do just that. We will stand firm."
He did not directly address whether European leaders had backed further strikes on Russian refineries, instead reiterating Ukraine's right to defend itself.
Zelenskyy accuses Putin of blocking peace efforts
The Ukrainian president said Ukraine remained committed to ending the war through negotiations but accused Putin of having no genuine interest in a peace agreement.
"Putin does not want negotiations right now, in any format," he said, describing Moscow's rhetoric as "a parody of a genuine desire to end the war".
"He does not want the war to end. I am convinced that this is why even the Donbas is too small for him."
Zelenskyy warns against easing sanctions on Russia
Zelenskyy also warned that easing restrictions on Russian diesel could lead to further concessions, undermining Western efforts to limit Moscow's ability to finance its war against Ukraine.
"In my view, we cannot accept these diesel deals, these agreements, because gas deals will follow. I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, sanctions will be lifted on other things as well," he said.
"It will all come down to the banking system, individuals, and the chemical industry."
He also voiced concern over the future of frozen Russian assets, suggesting they could be at risk if Western countries continued to make concessions to Moscow.
"If I do not defend this, who will do it for us? I mean diplomatically," Zelenskyy said.
European leaders have meanwhile sought to maintain pressure on Moscow despite Washington's decision to ease some sanctions.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Friday that the EU would not lift its sanctions until Russia ended the war. European Council President António Costa called for increased pressure on Moscow rather than further concessions.

articles.title: Policing of France’s school protests clouds Macron’s final months and sparks uproar - AP News
articles.summary: Policing of France’s school protests clouds Macron’s final months and sparks uproar  AP NewsFrance’s Students Won’t Back Down  The NationAre student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?  BBCFour graphs to understand the state of France's school system  Le Monde.frFrench police accused over war-like injuries to teenagers in school protests | France  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
PARIS (AP) — On one side, legions of determined teenagers protesting for their future by blockading schools and taking part in marches that have sometimes spiraled into violence.
On the other, one of the largest internal security forces in Europe, deployed by the government of an unpopular and outgoing president.
The result, playing out almost daily outside high schools and on the streets of France, is a nationwide storm of unrest. The mayhem of recent weeks — with mass arrests and hundreds of injured — has sparked an uproar in a country steeped in a centuries-old culture of protest. Even some police have turned on the government’s handling of the demonstrations.
Discontent shrouds Macron’s final months
For President Emmanuel Macron, who leaves office in May, it’s hardly the dream ending to his decade in power. He has faced a succession of protest movements that sapped his popularity and fueled broad criticism of how his ministers use police against demonstrators.
With the high schoolers, the outcry has grown particularly loud. That’s partly because the vast majority of the 8,000 people arrested in recent weeks are under 18 and because police riot-control weapons are blamed for life-changing injuries suffered by some young teens.
The protesters’ push for better-resourced schools, particularly in poorer Paris suburbs and other cities and towns, also has a sympathetic audience as France hurts from record poverty and record public debt.
But police complain that they’re facing violent rioters who are latching onto the protests and using the crowds as cover to attack officers, pelting them with rocks, fireworks and other projectiles and wreaking havoc with fires, vandalism and other destruction. By the government’s count, more than 900 officers and more than 150 teachers and other school staffers have been injured. More demonstrations, by a variety of groups with broader complaints beyond schools, are planned Saturday.
French history partly explains why protests are veering into confrontations between riot police and some demonstrators who come ready to fight in masks and black clothes, says Walid Hrar, a police officer and union representative in the northern suburbs of Paris.
“This is the country of the French Revolution. Everyone boasts about it, in fact. Some political parties don’t hesitate to say that we need to disobey the law. That’s what Robespierre and other revolutionaries taught us in 1789,” he said.
“France always tends to react rather than anticipate,” he added. “In other words, we’re always going to extremes.”
Attention focusing on police weaponry
The police have drawn sharp scrutiny for their efforts to control crowds using a variety of so-called non-lethal weaponry, particularly grenades and other projectiles, but also tear gas, water cannons and riot shields equipped with powerful strobe lights.
“We’re sending poorly equipped, untrained public security police officers to violent demonstrations who are likely to become agitated very quickly out of anger and fear,” said Jean-Marie Godard, an author who specializes in French policing.
Hrar said some of his police colleagues “aren’t specialized in crowd control and aren’t equipped for it. We send them in because we need the manpower, so we have officers wearing uniforms that aren’t flame-resistant. And if you’re hit by a firework mortar and your uniform isn’t flame-resistant, you can catch fire. We also have officers with worn-out helmets. We have shields that aren’t suitable.”
He said officers who haven’t been given permission to use riot-control projectiles and grenades sometimes struggle to keep attackers at a safe distance.
“So unfortunately we make do,” he said. “You’ll inevitably end up in direct physical confrontation. When that happens, there are injuries on both sides.”
His Alliance police union announced this week that it is filing a legal complaint against the state, accusing it of endangering lives. It alleged that officers are being issued with vague and contradictory orders, leaving them “isolated, betrayed, abandoned, exposed to violence.”
Probes of alleged misconduct grow
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said this week that security forces have used crowd-control weapons at least 18,000 times during the protests — mostly smoke and tear gas but also projectiles and grenades.
They include a deafening launcher-fired grenade that Nunez said was used “about 40 times” before he suspended its deployment against high schoolers, after a 15-year-old lost a hand.
“All this equipment, all these forces, all these intermediate weapons, are used whenever necessary, with proportionality, to mark an escalation of the response, to keep people at a distance or sometimes to put them out of action,” he said.
The minister said rules governing the use of riot-control projectiles are “very clear, very strict.”
“We avoid everything above the neck,” he said.
Still, an officer suspected of firing a round that partially blinded a 16-year-old was this week charged with aggravated violence.
That case is among a growing number of investigations — totaling 36 as of Tuesday — into alleged police misconduct.
Four involve “mutilating injuries,” another six involve “significant injuries” and others are for “blows, insults and suspected sexual assaults” and include the case of an officer accused of attempting to drown a protester, Nunez said.
Expert says different groups get different policing
France has more than 250,000 police and gendarmes.
Sebastian Roché, a policing specialist at France’s National Center for Scientific Research, said their use can depend on the political needs of the government, which commands them. Officers have been less forgiving with the teenagers than they previously were with farmers, a powerful lobby in France, who doused government buildings with manure, blocked roads and set fires.
“It’s the political definition of the movement that defines the police response,” Roché said.
Public perceptions of the police also change and are influenced by what people see on social media, said Hrar, who noted that officers were applauded for their bravery during terror attacks in 2015.
“When you bombard people every single day with images of police intervening with batons, shields and tear gas, you’re inevitably going to create a negative impression.”
___
McNeil reported from Brussels.

articles.title: One Singapore ship was sunk, but here's why others are still transiting the Strait of Hormuz - CNBC
articles.summary: One Singapore ship was sunk, but here's why others are still transiting the Strait of Hormuz  CNBCTwo ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles amid surge in attacks  ReutersIran Guards say oil tanker exploded after hitting mine in 'unauthorized' route through Hormuz  The Times of IsraelShips in Strait of Hormuz still face "indiscriminate attacks," maritime monitor warns  CBS NewsShip attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports ...
articles.full_text:
Commercial vessels are likely to continue navigating the perilous Strait of Hormuz despite the sinking of a Singapore-flagged container ship this week, as strong demand for Middle Eastern energy and lucrative shipping opportunities keep some operators willing to brave escalating attacks, maritime experts said.
The latest attacks on two Singapore-flagged container ships have heightened concerns over the safety of commercial shipping through one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints. But analysts say the incidents are unlikely to bring remaining shipping activity through the Strait to a halt, even as major container lines largely stay away.
Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said shipping companies were likely to continue seeking opportunities to transit the strait despite heightened security threats.
“I don’t see in the short term, that Singapore flagged ships or Singapore shipping companies would necessarily avoid taking the transit if there is an opportunity,” Koh told CNBC.
His comments follow attacks on two Singapore-registered container ships, GFS Pride and GFS Giselle, this week. GFS Pride sank after being struck by a projectile and catching fire, while GFS Giselle was damaged. Crew members from both vessels were reported safe.
Crossings through the Strait of Hormuz fell to 131 in the week ended Oct. 14, from 176 the previous week, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler, although the decline cannot be attributed solely to the latest incidents.
Dimitris Ampatzidis, maritime risk and compliance manager at Kpler, said the attacks underscored Iran’s continuing ability to threaten commercial vessels, with the risks extending beyond oil and gas transportation.
Koh said shipping companies around the world have continued looking for opportunities to navigate the Strait since the conflict erupted, with some operators prepared to accept higher risks and costs.
Strong demand for oil, particularly from Asia, continues to provide an incentive for tanker operators to transport energy supplies from the Persian Gulf, even as security threats complicate voyages.
Some operators may be willing to take their chances even if doing so involves paying a premium, Koh said.
Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan offered an example of how higher oil prices could make voyages through Hormuz commercially worthwhile despite the dangers.
Speaking at the Milken Institute Asia Summit last week, Balakrishnan recounted a conversation with an unnamed Gulf counterpart who said his country was earning more from oil exports than before the war by operating a so-called “Hormuz shuttle” involving about 20 very large crude carriers.
The vessels were effectively self-insured against attacks, according to the official’s account, with higher crude prices making the voyages financially worthwhile despite the risks.
“Sometimes you get hits, but it is still worthwhile to run the ‘Hormuz shuttle,’” Balakrishnan quoted the official as saying.
Despite the risks, vessels continue to transit the Strait, reflecting its commercial importance, particularly for energy shipments to Asian markets, Ampatzidis said.
However, further attacks could deter more operators from making the passage, with the impact likely to differ depending on vessel type and individual companies’ assessments of the risks, he added.
The Singapore Shipping Association also played down the prospect of a broad withdrawal of commercial shipping from the region, suggesting operators would instead adapt to changing trade conditions.
“Rather than signalling a broad withdrawal from the region, these developments are more likely to result in adjustments to trading patterns as markets respond to shifts in the supply and demand of goods and energy,” said association president TS Teo.
Shipowners would continue weighing commercial considerations against security developments and crew safety when making operational decisions, he added.
While some operators remain willing to transit Hormuz, much of the global container shipping industry has already adjusted its networks to avoid the strait.
Jayendu Krishna, a director at Drewry Maritime Advisors, said none of the major container shipping lines had resumed services through Hormuz since suspending operations following the outbreak of the war in February. Only some regional operators have continued sporadic services, generally using smaller feeder vessels.
That means the immediate impact of the latest attacks on container shipping could be limited, he said.
However, a further escalation into the Gulf of Oman could pose a more serious threat to regional supply chains, particularly if it disrupts alternative ports like Khorfakkan in the United Arab Emirates and Oman’s Sohar that have become critical gateways for cargo entering Gulf countries.
“If the Gulf of Oman became a zone of kinetic activity, a significant part of supplies to the Gulf countries would be cut off, since Khorfakkan and Sohar have been a lifeline for them,” Krishna said.

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and his British counterpart Wes Streeting held a meeting at the Pentagon in Washington on Thursday. The sides discussed defense burden-sharing in NATO, defense spending and military cooperation, Anadolu Agency reports.
A greater role for Europe

He also outlined the concept of “NATO 3.0,” under which European members of the Alliance should take on greater responsibility for Europe’s conventional defense.

Spending and defense production
Streeting supported strengthening Europe’s role in its own defense and said that the United Kingdom is ready to more actively defend Europe and its interests. He thanked Trump for encouraging European countries to take their defense commitments more seriously.
The British representative said that the country is undertaking the largest sustained increase in defense spending since the end of the Cold War. At the same time, he stressed that not only the scale of investment matters, but also directing it toward effective capabilities and faster deployment of defense technologies.

articles.title: Beijing uses the South China Sea to corner Taiwan - GIS Reports
articles.summary: Beijing uses the South China Sea to corner Taiwan  GIS Reports
articles.full_text:
Maritime boundary disputes mask a bigger contest over Taiwan’s future.
GIS Radio
Listen to our AI-powered podcast for comprehensive insights.
- Beijing sees disputes as leverage, not territorial strife
- Manila is firm on border policy while pragmatic in economics with Beijing
- Japan’s growing security role could fill gaps from American downsizing
Behind China’s opposition to the Japan-Philippines negotiations on maritime borders lies its desire to expedite a resolution to the Taiwan question by fueling territorial disputes in the South China Sea.
Based on the so-called nine-dash line principle, Beijing claims sovereignty over approximately 90 percent of the resource-rich South China Sea, an area that overlaps with the exclusive economic zones (EEZs) of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam.
On July 12, 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague, Netherlands, found that China’s historical claims to the nine-dash line in the South China Sea lacked legal basis. However, the weight of this decision depends on the voluntary compliance and enforcement of the parties involved. The Chinese government has declared the arbitration worthless and maintains that the ruling disregards its historical rights in the sea. This has led to ongoing tension between China and affected countries, particularly the Philippines.
In late May 2026, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced that Japan and the Philippines had agreed to launch formal delimitation negotiations to set the limits of their overlapping exclusive economic zones and continental shelves in the waters east of Taiwan. Both sides hope to conclude these negotiations this year.
EEZs, territorial waters and continental shelves
In 1982, United Nations member states agreed to the Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), defining the legal framework for all marine and maritime activities, replacing the “freedom of the seas” concept from the 17th century. UNCLOS defines EEZs, territorial waters and continental shelves. China, Japan and the Philippines are signatories to the convention and have ratified it in their legislatures.
Territorial waters or seas give a nation full sovereignty – including control of navigation – over the waters out 12 nautical miles (22 kilometers) from its shores.
Exclusive economic zones stretch out a further 200 nautical miles (370 kilometers) from the edge of the territorial zone. A state has exclusive rights regarding the exploration and use of underwater and marine resources of the area, though in navigation terms, this part of the sea is itself considered international water.
A country’s continental shelf covers the seabed and subsoil of the submarine areas extending a minimum of 200 nautical miles (370 kilometers) from its coast, though it can be larger in some situations. Coastal nations have exclusive rights to explore and exploit the natural resources of their continental shelf, but do not own the territory.
The distance between Japan’s southwestern islands and the northernmost islands of the Philippines is less than 400 nautical miles, which naturally leads to overlapping claims regarding EEZs in waters east of Taiwan. Both countries hope to establish clear and peaceful boundaries in accordance with international law to clearly regulate maritime activities such as fishing and resource management while avoiding ambiguities. The delimitation negotiations are part of a broader effort to enhance bilateral trust, intelligence sharing and maritime security in the Indo-Pacific region. It is also designed as a move against China’s claims of the maritime territories in the respective region.
Beijing strongly protests these negotiations, claiming that the bilateral consultation process is illegal and the area in question infringes upon China’s asserted maritime rights. However, under UNCLOS Articles 74 and 83, adjacent coastal states have the right to resolve overlapping boundary issues through bilateral negotiations. If this model of bilateral negotiation and territorial demarcation takes hold, any two countries could team up to carve up the sea, specifically, areas claimed by a third country such as China. Nevertheless, Taiwan will be de facto “sandwiched” through the Tokyo-Manila negotiations.
China’s primary concern is not the specific territorial disputes in the South China Sea; rather, it is using this issue to expedite a resolution to the Taiwan question.
The Philippines’ strategy: Strong on territory, flexible with economics
Since many Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member states are located around the South China Sea and have made sovereignty claims that differ from China’s, the intergovernmental forum has been working since 2013 to negotiate with China a rules-based Code of Conduct in the South China Sea, aimed at easing tensions and preventing conflicts. Yet due to China’s obstruction and to internal disagreements within ASEAN itself, these negotiations have yet to be concluded.
The Philippines and Vietnam are among the countries most actively promoting the protection of their territorial waters and EEZs. Other claimants, however, are adopting approaches that avoid offending China’s interests. For example, Malaysia recently has supported the One China principle and hinted that it might support China’s use of force to seize Taiwan. Meanwhile, Indonesia, despite having overlapping maritime sovereignty claims with China, conducted joint military exercises with China in August of this year in the sensitive waters east of Taiwan. In this regard, the Japan-Philippines negotiations are a reaction to ASEAN’s inaction in the face of escalating tensions between the South China Sea claimant states and China.
Disputed territories
China and the Philippines have already clashed in the South China Sea. The most recent incident occurred on July 24, 2026, when a Philippine government vessel entered the waters around Scarborough Shoal, a coral atoll in the disputed South China Sea waters. There have been more violent standoffs as well. In 2024, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said in his State of the Nation Address that the country “will not bow to bullies.”
To this end, the Philippines has decided to strengthen its military capabilities. Given the vast disparity in military strength with China, Manila has opted for asymmetric warfare, actively developing drones and missile patrol vessels to enhance its strike and surveillance capabilities. It has also joined forces with other countries to uphold UNCLOS. The Philippines, Japan and the United States recently completed a round of joint defense exercises in the South China Sea. Meanwhile, the U.S.-Philippines Mutual Defense Treaty provides a potential foundation for collective deterrence.
At the same time, Manila is strengthening its economic cooperation with both Washington and Tokyo. The Philippines has formally joined the Silicon Prosperity Initiative, a hub that serves as the backbone of the Luzon Economic Corridor, a multinational infrastructure and investment initiative linking Subic Bay, Clark, metro Manila and Batangas in the Philippines. The development program is promoted by Washington, Manila and Tokyo. The U.S. will provide $100 million in aid for its construction.
However, despite Manila’s tensions with China and its hard line against Beijing on territorial issues, the Marcos administration has also demonstrated diplomatic pragmatism and is cautiously cooperating with China in other areas. This approach appears to align with China’s short-term strategy.
President Marcos has publicly stated that he remains optimistic about economic relations between the two countries, with the war in Iran being a catalyst with a direct negative impact on the Philippines’ energy and fertilizer supplies. On March 17, the Philippines requested that China not interrupt fertilizer supplies. Chinese leaders agreed, ensuring the country’s needs for spring planting were met. The Philippines was also able to procure diesel fuel from China. President Marcos publicly thanked Beijing for its assistance. Currently, China and the Philippines are negotiating joint energy exploration efforts.
Japan’s role is growing
Although Japan is not a claimant in the South China Sea, it is a stakeholder in the rules-based order in the First Island Chain, the strategic geographic line of Pacific archipelagos including Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines. In July of this year, Japan and 13 other countries issued a joint statement marking the 10th anniversary of the international arbitration tribunal’s rejection of Beijing’s broad sovereignty claims over disputed areas in the South China Sea. Under the framework of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, the leaders of Japan and the Philippines agreed to launch negotiations on the General Security of Military Information Agreement as a first step toward future intelligence sharing and to explore the possibility of Japan transferring a warship to the Philippines.
This move by Japan is directly linked to Tokyo’s decision to shift its military from a postwar role of exclusive defense to a new presence capable of proactive deterrence and transnational intervention. This development also directly aligns with U.S. President Donald Trump’s gradual scaling back of the U.S. military presence in Asia and elsewhere, while simultaneously demanding that its traditional East Asian allies, like those in Europe, increase their defense spending. For varying reasons, countries like Indonesia and Vietnam welcome Japan’s expanding military, economic and diplomatic influence as a strategic third option.

articles.summary: NATO convenes urgent meeting over drone attacks on vessels in Black Sea  Цензор.НЕТ
articles.full_text:
Next week, ambassadors from NATO member countries will meet to discuss drone attacks on ships off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria.
According to Censor.NET, France24 reports on this.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated that the Alliance will continue to work closely with its allies in the Black Sea region and will adjust its deterrence and defense measures as needed.
Romania is requesting equipment to counter new threats
Speaking to reporters in Brussels, Romanian President Nicușor Dan announced that NATO will hold a meeting to address the increasing number of drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.
According to him, Romania needs "equipment to address new types of challenges."
Incidents involving civilian vessels have become more frequent off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania. This is likely related to Russia's war against Ukraine.
What led up to this?
- On the night of October 13, drones attacked two merchant ships off the Bulgarian coast.
- In addition to the sunken vessel, three drones struck the Maltese-flagged cargo ship CHELSEA 3, which is registered in Odesa and, according to Bulgarian media reports, belongs to Ukraine.
- All 15 crew members of the CHELSEA 3, including seven Ukrainians, were evacuated to the port of Varna. Five sailors required medical attention.
- Following the attacks, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev convened an emergency meeting of the Security Council and announced his intention to demand an explanation from Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova.
- At the same time, Bulgarian authorities emphasized that there is currently no conclusive evidence regarding the origin of the drones.
- Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sibiga stated that Ukrainian and Azerbaijani citizens were injured as a result of attacks on merchant ships near Bulgarian territorial waters.
- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attacks on civilian vessels in the Black Sea.
